guides.h:
A Culinary Artillery: Cooking 100 - Your Tools
The font of creation

Introduction
This mod adds a variety of cooking utensils and mechanics that don't do anything on their own but require another mod such as Expanded Foods in order to fully utilize. This mod is ONLY a library for other mods!

Syntax
To eliminate confusion, certain vocabulary will be defined here. When a guide using A Culinary Artillery uses these words, they are in a direct and specific manner.

Bake - Place an item in a hot clay oven.
Boil - Place the items in a Saucepan or Cauldron on a hot firepit.
Cook - Place an item in a firepit's upper slot.
Dry Age - Place the item on a Meat Rack by right-clicking, then wait for it to dry age. If the meat starts to rot before aging, it will NOT age.
Knead - Place items in the top 6 slots of the Mixing Bowl and right-click to output an item.
Mix - Place a cooking pot in the lower-left slot of a Mixing Bowl, then add food to the top 6 slots and right-click to output a meal.
Press - Place a stack of items in the Fruit Press and right-click to begin pressing.

Expanded Food - A special kind of food that can have multiple nutrition types.

NEW COOKING BLOCKS

Bottles
Made from clay or glass, bottles are capable of holding liquids in the same manner as bowls and can be placed in the world or on shelves or bottle racks. Can be used to ferment drinks or for liquid consumption.
Meat Rack
Items with the 'meathookable' attribute can be Dried on a meat rack. This process ages the meat and boosts its nutritional value. Non-food items can be hung from the rack, such as mini-cauldrons, saucepans, and meat cleavers.
Mixing Bowl
Vital for creating many Expanded Foods. Can take 6 slots of food or liquid, then Knead it together into a new item. Placing a pot into it allows you to Mix certain meals. It can be mechanically powered by connecting an axle to the top or bottom of the block.
The mixing bowl can be locked with Ctrl+Right mouse on the bowl. When locked, it will only accept the ingredients that were in it, and in those specific slots. It cannot automatically accept liquids.
Saucepan
Functions somewhat similarly to a bucket, but you can place it onto a firepit to Boil the liquids inside. In order to Boil something in the saucepan, it must be placed into its slots. It is capable of turning some solids into liquids, and turning some liquids into solids. Press Ctrl+Shift+Right mouse to place a lid on it, slightly increasing the lifespan of liquids within.
Cauldron
The cauldron is a larger version of the saucepan and is also used to Boil liquids. It is created by pouring liquid metal into a clay cauldron mold. You can also place a lid on the cauldron, but it is more effective than the saucepan's lid.
Spile
Jam this into a tree and place a bucket or saucepan beneath it to collect sap from the tree during certain times of the year. Does nothing on its own, another mod such as Expanded Foods is required to add new liquids.

NEW COOKING ITEMS

Rolling Pin
Carved from logs or smithed, rolling pins can be used to flatten foods such as meat and pasta dough. They are also a weak weapon.

EGG CHANGES
Any egg can be cracked into a bowl or bucket. Partially cracking it with Ctrl+Right mouse results in 0.1 L of Liquid Egg White and an Egg Yolk item, which can be cracked again for 0.1 L of Liquid Egg Yolk. These can be used as breading and will have more uses in the future. You can mix these liquids or fully crack an egg with Ctrl+Shift+Right mouse to get 0.1 L of Liquid Egg, which is used in place of raw eggs in many recipes. Once an egg is cracked, it results in Eggshells, which can be used as fertilizer or animal feed.

Mixing
The popular stereotype of the chef is that of a skeptic and a pessimist. Nothing could be further from the truth! Gastronomists must be optimists at heart, in order to block out the incessant chorus of those who say "It cannot be done."

To craft a mixing bowl is to approach a culinary event horizon. Through the labor of creation, infinite possibilies awaken. Once a mixing bowl is placed, Right mouse it in order to open the menu. There are 6 slots at the top - these are where ingredients are placed. The lower-right slot is the output slot, where finished foods or meals are placed. The lower-left slot is only used when mixing meals, and is reserved for the cooking pot.
NOTE: To knead something is to create it in the mixing bowl without a cooking pot, outputting an item. To mix something is to create it in the mixing bowl WITH a cooking pot, outputting a meal.

Once your ingredients are placed, either hold Right mouse on the mixing bowl, or if you have a powered mixing bowl then you may utilize mechanical power through the bottom of the machine. This will start kneading your ingredients together. If your output slot is full, then the kneaded creation will be output directly next to the mixing bowl (hopefully into a hopper instead of the dirty ground).

Mixing meals works slightly differently. Unlike kneading foods (and like when creating meals in a cooking pot), a meal can only be mixed with exact ingredient proportions. In order to mix a meal, you MUST have a cooking pot in the lower-left slot, and it will ALWAYS be output into the lower-right slot - never dumped out of the mixing bowl. You can only have one cooking pot in an input/output slot at a time, they do not stack.

TIP: You can click Ctrl+Right mouse on the top of the mixing bowl to "lock" its ingredients in place so they may not be changed.

Simmering
What actually transpires beneath the veil of a cauldron lid? Decent people shouldn't think too much about that.

A wide world of culinary options is at your fingertips, once you learn how to throw something into a hot pot of water (or other liquids). In order to start simmering food, fire a saucepan. Alternately, cast a cauldron or small cauldron or purchase one from a Kitchenware Trader. Once you have your new cooking implement, place it into a firepit, this will add 4 "simmering" slots to the firepit inventory, similar to when making meals. Simmering ALWAYS requires a liquid, and anywhere from 1 to 4 slots may be required to make a new food item.
All used slots must hold an equal amount of portion, and portion sizes for any given item may be found directly on the item's page, under the "Created by Simmering" section (see gelatin for example).

A simmer container can output items in two different ways: Solid items will be placed into the output slot and may be directly grabbed with your hands, as your container remains in its slot. Liquid items are placed into your simmer container, which is then moved from the input slot on into the output slot and must be removed from that slot in order to be used further.

Alchemy allows you to brew potions that enhance your abilities, grant utility effects, and more. There are three tiers of potions, each requiring progressively more advanced equipment.

Tier 1 - Edible Herbs: The earliest form of alchemy. Only a mortar & pestle required.

Tier 2 - Medium Potions: Liquid potions brewed in a cauldron firepit. Requires copper age, with a barrel, a cauldron and wooden stirring spoon.

Tier 3 - Strong Potions: Can you handle my strongest potions? Requires herb racks, glassworking and aqua vitae.

Weapon Coating: Apply potions to your weapons and arrows to deliver their effects on hit.

Throwable Flasks: Throw filled flasks to splash potion effects onto all creatures in range on impact.

The Alchemy mod is highly configurable. I highly reccomend you use the mod ConfigLib if you want to change anything about this mod, the are hundreds of different config values for you to adjust.
If you have any suggestions or find any bugs, preferably let me know on the official Vintage Story discord in the alchemy mod thread, or just leave a comment on the mod page.

Weapon coating lets you apply a potion onto a melee weapon or onto arrows so the potion's effect is delivered to whatever you hit. Great for making a healing club for an ally, or poisoning your enemies.

What you need:
A coating source held in your OFF hand. This can be an edible herb ball (uses one herb) or a potion flask(uses 0.25 L).
A coatable item held in your MAIN hand which is any melee weapon or a arrow (both configurable).

How to apply a coating:
Hold the coating source in your off hand and the weapon or arrows in your main hand, then hold Shift + Right-click and keep holding for a couple of seconds.

Quick coating with a barrel:
Place a weapon or a stack of arrows into a barrel of potion to coat them instantly. Weapons are coated to max charge and arrow stacks all at once.

Melee weapons:
Each coat adds one charge, up to a maximum (5 by default). Every melee hit on a living creature spends one charge and applies the potion effect.

Projectiles:
Projectiles such as arrows are coated individually rather than by charges. A coated projectile delivers its effect to the first creature it hits. By default it's only arrows.

Strength:
Coating effects are a fraction of the strength of drinking the same potion (90% by default). If enabled, potions that aren't healing or spiked oil can be used but will only work on players.

A weapon can only hold one type of potion at a time at one strength, so hit something to clear a coating before switching potions.

Edible herbs are the simplest form of alchemy and require no metal tools.

Craft a mortar and pestle to get started. There is a wood variant or stone variant that has greater durability. Gather herbs, flowers, poisonous/psychedelic mushrooms, and horsetail from the wild.

Grind poisonous/psychedelic mushrooms and horsetail together in the mortar and pestle to create a basic potion base. Then grind your choice of herbs or flowers into a weak potion base. Combine the weak potion base and the basic potion base in a crafting grid to create an edible herb ball.

Edible herbs are consumed directly for a weak effect.

Edible herbs: Archer, Potent, Purging, Settling, Hunter, Looter, Fighter, Miner, Spiked, Predator, Healing, Scentmask, Speed, Vitality

Medium potions are liquid brews cooked in a brewing cauldron. They are more effective than edible herbs and they are stored in flasks.

You will need: a brewing cauldron, a wooden stirring spoon attached to the cauldron, a barrel for making potion tea, and flasks to store and drink the finished potions (You can drink from other liquid containers if config is changed, although flasks handle potion drinking better).

Cauldron Setup:
Place the cauldron in the world, then right-click it with dry grass in hand, followed by four right-clicks with firewood in hand. The cauldron is now ready to use.

Step 1 - Make Potion Tea:
Seal a barrel with 1 basic potion base and 2 litres of water. After 24 hours it will turn into potion tea. This is a key ingredient for all liquid potions.

Step 2 - Brew the Potion:
Place 1 weak potion base and 1 litre of potion tea into the cauldron, attach a wooden stirring spoon, then light the fire beneath. The cauldron will cook the mixture into a medium potion.

Step 3 - Fill Flasks:
Use a flask or bowl to take the finished potion from the cauldron output slot.

A warning about jugs: jugs only move 0.3 litres of liquid at a time, so filling or emptying one at a cauldron takes a painful number of interactions. Use flasks or bowls with the cauldron instead.

Utility potions are brewed the same way using their respective bases with 1 litre of potion tea.

Medium potions: Archer's Flask, Potent Oil, Purging Brew, Settling Brew, Hunter's Delight, Looter's Delight, Fighter's Flask, Miner's Flask, Spiked Oil, Predator Pheromones, Healing Oil, Scent Mask, Sprinter's Flask, Vitality Flask
Utility potions: Water Breathing Flask, Glow Flask, Nutrition Flask, Featherfall Flask, Spider Flask, Growth Flask, Shrinking Flask, Warmth Flask

The stronger utility flasks (recall, stability and reshape) use the Tier 3 recipe instead, see Tier 3 - Strong Potions. Which tier each utility flask uses can be changed in the config.

Strong potions are the most powerful of brews, requiring glassworking and aqua vitae in addition to the equipment from Tier 2.

Additional requirements: a glass stirring spoon (required instead of a wooden spoon), a herb rack for drying your herbs, and aqua vitae. There are many wood and metal variants of herb racks available.

Step 1 - Dry Your Herbs:
Hang fresh herb or flower raw cuttings on a herb rack. They will slowly dry into dried cuttings. Cuttings are unlikely to spoil while on the rack.

Step 2 - Cook the Dried Cuttings:
Cook the dried cuttings on a firepit or in a clay oven to create cooked cuttings.

Step 3 - Make the Strong Potion Base:
Combine cooked cuttings in a crafting grid to create a strong potion base.

Step 4 - Brew the Potion:
Place 1 strong potion base, 0.25 litres of aqua vitae, and 0.75 litres of potion tea into the cauldron. Attach a glass stirring spoon and light the fire. Potion tea is still made the same way as in Tier 2 (basic potion base + 2L water in a barrel, sealed for 24 hours).

Strong potions: Archer's Flask, Potent Oil, Purging Brew, Settling Brew, Hunter's Delight, Looter's Delight, Fighter's Flask, Miner's Flask, Spiked Oil, Predator Pheromones, Healing Oil, Scent Mask, Sprinter's Flask, Vitality Flask
Utility potions: Recall Flask, Stability Flask, Reshape Flask

These utility flasks are brewed like any other strong potion, using their own base with 0.25 litres of aqua vitae and 0.75 litres of potion tea. The remaining utility flasks use the Tier 2 recipe, see Tier 2 - Medium Potions. Which tier each utility flask uses can be changed in the config.

Throwable flasks are vessels filled with a potion that shatter on impact, splashing their effect onto all living creatures within range. They come in two variants: glass and ceramic.

Glass Throwable Flasks:
Available in many colours depending on the ore used (clear quartz, olivine, amethyst, rose quartz, smoky quartz, and others).
See: Glass Throwable Flask

Ceramic Throwable Flasks:
Clay-formed using blue, fire, or red clay colour based on cooking method.
See: Ceramic Throwable Flask

Filling:
Fill a throwable flask the same way as any potion flask - tap right-click on a liquid container. The flask holds exactly one dose.

Throwing:
Hold the filled flask in your main hand and right-click to wind up and release the throw.

On impact:
The flask shatters and applies the potion effect to all living creatures within the splash radius (2.5m by default, configurable). Effects are applied at 50% strength by default (configurable). Only potions permitted for weapon coating can be applied this way but still can be thrown.

If thrown into liquids the flask will slow rapidly dropping as an intact item without shattering and preserving its contents if its slow enough. Doesn't apply potion effects under water.

A glossary of every effect a potion that can be applied and what each one does.

Many effects come in three strengths, shown on the flask as weak, medium and strong. A higher strength only increases the size of the effect, not how long it lasts.

Ranged accuracy: steadies your aim with bows and slings.
Ranged damage: increases damage from arrows and sling rocks.
Ranged speed: speeds up drawing and loading ranged weapons.
Melee damage: increases damage with melee weapons.
Walk speed: increases movement speed on foot.
Hunger rate: changes how fast your food bar drains; a higher rate hungers you faster, a lower rate slower.
Healing effectiveness: affects bandages apply time (config can be used to effect potions drink/eat time as well). It for some reason doesn't change your natural regeneration or the amount healed last checked on v1.22.3 of Vintage story.
Max health: raises your maximum health for the duration.
Restore health: heals you over time.
Poison: damages you over time and ignores armour.
Mining speed: breaks stones and ores faster. Doesn't affect dirt.
Ore amount: increases ore from mined ore blocks.
Animal loot: increases drops from harvesting carcasses. Doesn't apply to rust creatures.
Forage amount: increases drops from foraged berries, mushrooms and ground forage.
Wild crop: increases drops from harvesting wild plants.
Gears from metal pile: increases rusty gears recovered from metal piles.
Vessel contents: increases loot from broken storage vessels.
Animal seek range: changes how far creatures notice you; lowering it hides you, raising it draws them toward you.

Utility effects come in only weak strength and last for the duration shown on the flask:
Glow: you emit light.
Water breathing: your oxygen stays full underwater.
Warmth: your body temperature will not fall below normal.
Temporal stability: a one-time boost to your temporal stability.
Nutrition: evens out your nutrition across all food groups. Usually with a cost of overall nutrition loss.
Recall: teleports you to your spawn point.
Reshape: lets you re-open character selection once with the .charsel command.
Growth: increases your size until death or drink purging brew (or disconnect if RetainEffectsOnDisconnect is off).
Shrinking: decreases your size until death or drink purging brew (or disconnect if RetainEffectsOnDisconnect is off).
Featherfall: reduces fall damage.
Spider: lets you climb any surface.
Flight: lets you fly freely. You cannot mount anything when the effect is active.

Side effects when drank (a cost paid only when applied):
Damage taken / health restored: a brew may hurt or heal you.
Intoxication: a drunkenness effect, shown as a percentage of maximum.
Psychedelic: a hallucinogenic effect, shown as a percentage of maximum.
Saturation: a change to your food bar level.

Other mods may change how these effects behave and this list may fall out of date.

Class guide
Press C for traits and handbook links of your class!

Miner
Go mining
- really high mining speed
- really high ore yield
- prefers melee combat

Farmer
Farm and harvest crops
- high yield of harvested crops
- able to craft fertilizer
- prefers ranged combat

Lumberjack
Get wood, make sticks and charcoal
- high yield of wood from trees
- able to craft sticks and a backpack to carry more wood
- more yield from coal pits
- prefers melee combat

Carpenter
Build windmills and produce boards
- advantage in mill-crafting
- can craft cheaper boards
- prefers melee combat

Potter
Get peat and clay, craft mortar, plaster and refractory bricks
- high yield of peat and clay
- able to craft cheaper items that need clay
- fast digging
- prefers melee combat

Mason
Mine rocks, craft stone blocks
- cheaper crafting recipes for most stone related things
- drops more rocks from stone

Blacksmith
Make repair kits and steel
- makes repair kits for cheaper armor repairs
- prefers melee combat
- on RP Patch the only one to craft iron doors for steel making

Wanderer
Go on an adventure, forage everything you see
- really high foraging yield (berries, mushrooms..)
- can make bigger backpacks
- generally an explorer class
- don’t try to kill animals

Butcher the cattle, cook the cattle
- can make bigger pots
- can make better kitchen fuels
- should breed and kill animals
- is meant to wear plate armor
- imagine him in combat as a tank and at home as a cook and butcher
- prefers melee combat

Stay at home and work. Send your friends out to get materials

- is meant to stay at the base
- is not good at anything else besides this
- prefers melee combat

Make medicine, feed medicine to your friends

- good at foraging

- prefers ranged combat

Do whatever you want

Shoot everything that moves
