This mod is built with Expanded Foods in mind. Certain blocks (for example, the Barrel Racks) will only Cure liquids if Expanded Foods is installed. Without it, they still apply freshness-related buffs, but no curing will occur.

Block Buffs
Some blocks offer buffs to perish rate, curing rate, or drying rate. If a block has such a buff, it will be shown directly in the block tooltip when you hover over it. These tooltips may also display helpful quality-of-life features - for example, Seed Bins show the nutrient type required by the seeds they contain.

Ice Cooling Mechanic
Blocks like the Cooling Cabinet and Meat Freezer provide a small unbuffed freshness bonus while their doors are closed. Leaving them open negates this benefit, so always keep them shut!
These blocks can be further enhanced with Cut Ice. Ice is placed in a dedicated drawer, melts over time, and must be replaced regularly. The buff only applies when both the main compartment and the ice drawer are closed, so double-check those doors!

Ice Keepers
Ice Keepers are specialized storage blocks for Cut Ice. They can hold up to 16 stacks of Cut Ice and, while stored inside, prevent it from melting entirely. This makes them useful for keeping a large supply of ice ready for your cooling blocks.

Baskets for Decoration and Preservation
Baskets are primarily decorative and not meant for bulk storage. However, when placed inside a Cooling Cabinet, they inherit its freshness buffs (iced or not), making them a stylish way to preserve food a bit longer.

Further Information
Not all containers accept every item. Each block has a dedicated handbook entry that lists the valid item types and, when relevant, the mods those items come from.

Interactions
Most interactions are shown via World Interactions (floating in-game hints). For example: adding items to baskets, closing cabinet doors, or filling drawers with ice.
Some interactions are not displayed, particularly when baskets are inside cabinets. You can still place items directly into a basket (right-click with the correct item, or hold CTRL to insert multiple). With an empty hand, holding CTRL will take out one item at a time.

Enjoy your decorated, functional kitchens!

Starter Survival Guide
Survival: The Art of not dying

Note: This guide is purposely kept short, additional guides are in the Guides tab on the left and a comprehensive survival guide can be found on the wiki.

First tools
Find flint or hard stones. They can often be found loose on the ground. When you have 2 of them, Shift + Right mouse-click to place one on the ground to begin knapping.

Expanding inventory
Your starting inventory has 10 slots, you can also carry up to 4 baskets or other containers. The most basic one, the hand basket, requires 10 cattails. Harvest cattails from reeds or papyrus, then hit 'E' to open your inventory to craft. The crafting recipe is on the hand basket page.

Finding food
An easy food source is berries from berry bushes. If you are feeling adventurous, attempt to hunt and kill an animal. Cooked cattail roots are a good emergency food. Keep an eye open for crops, they will be valuable food sources in the longer term. Once you found clay, be sure to get into meal cooking to greatly improve your nutrition intake.

Fire / Light
Knap a knife and use it to gather grass. Place the grass on the ground, add 4 pieces of fire wood and ignite it with a Firestarter. You can now use the firepit to cook roots and meat, or light torches that can be made from sticks and dry grass.

Combat
To hunt and kill in the stone age, craft yourself a spear or wooden club. Put together some improvised armor for some very basic protection.

Shelter
It is a good idea to build a small shelter before the night sets. Useful stone age building materials are cob, soil, packed dirt, cobble stone from ruins and logs.

Preparing for winter
On standard worlds, you have about 70 in-game days to prepare for the cold season, where you can no longer grow crops and wild animals yield less meat, and you can also suffer from the cold. It's recommended to stock up on food by preserving it and keeping animals.

For further progression, see Progression Guide.

Progression Guide
The desire to learn is the basis of all human progress

Stone Age
Craft stone tools through knapping, make fire, forage for food and build a shelter. See also: Starter Survival Guide

Pottery Age
Learn and master pottery. Find and dig up some clay. Craft yourself clay vessels, for storage, pots and bowls, for cooking and eating meals, as well as a crucible and tool molds, to prepare for the copper age. This is also a good time to start farming.
A wood lamellar armor set (head, body, legs) provides some additional protection against low tier foes. Or gamboised armor is excellent if you have a lot of flax.

Early Copper Age
Time to craft a copper pickaxe and hammer! Clay form a pickaxe mold and hammer mold and fire it. Find 40 nuggets of copper. You can find them loose on the ground, which also indicate an underground deposit. You can also find them in cracked vessels, through panning sand and gravel or by purchasing them from traders. Acquire charcoal and smelt the copper on a firepit. See also: Smelting Guide. Pour the smelted copper into the pickaxe and hammer mold. The hammer allows you to crush copper ore, which you can collect using your shiny new copper pickaxe.

Late Copper Age
Mine enough copper deposits and create an anvil mold. Once you have cast an anvil, you will be able to create fine tools like a saw, which will let you craft wooden boards.
With boards you can, among other things, create shields, and barrels, which let you preserve vegetables and produce leather for leather armor.

Bronze Age
Acquire one of the 3 types of bronze:
- Tin bronze: Find tin ore and mix it with copper
- Bismuth bronze: Find zinc and bismuth ore, mix them with copper
- Black bronze: Find gold and silver ore, mix them with copper

Ways to find these ores:
- Tin: Underground, very rarely on the surface, from traders, rarely from cracked ore vessels or from panning.
- Zinc, bismuth: Underground, rarely from cracked ore vessels or from traders
- Gold, silver: Inside quartz deposits, but requires either bombs or a bronze pick to mine; rarely in cracked ore vessels

Use the prospecting pick, to help narrow down locations, when searching for underground ores.

Iron age
Find iron, mine iron-bearing ores and build a bloomery base and chimney from fired fireclay bricks. Make sure you have enough coal or charcoal. Place the iron ore nuggets and coal into the bloomery and then ignite it. About one in-game day later, the bloomery will stop burning and you can break it to acquire iron blooms. Iron blooms have to be worked on the anvil to create wrought iron ingots, which in turn can be worked into tools. The anvil must be bronze tier or higher. Ferrous metals need higher temperatures to be workable, so you'll also want a bellows to raise the temperature.

Refining iron blooms can be mechanized with a helve hammer.

The bloomery can also be used to make glass from quartz. Glass has decorative uses, can be used to craft lanterns, and you can create greenhouses to extend the types of crops you can farm.

Late iron age
If you have encountered meteoric iron along your journey and you have a firm grip on iron working, it might be wise to construct an iron anvil through smithing, which allows you to work meteoric iron, for a roughly 20% boost in tool durability.

Steel age
Steel tools grant a hefty bonus of 2.5x the durability compared to iron, but the creation of steel is a complex and time intensive process. Head over to the steelmaking guide once you feel ready to achieve this feat.

Knapping
Can't wait to get your hands on those essential stone age tools? Then keep on reading!

'Knapping' means chipping away at raw stones until they are in the shape of a tool head. To begin knapping, first collect 2 stones: either flints or loose stones of a hard type of stone (e.g. granite). With a stone or flint in your active hand slot, look at the ground and hold Shift + Right mouse (once for flint, or twice for any other stone) to place the stone to create a knapping surface. Some recipes are shown, click for the type of stone tool head you want to create. The shape will then be marked out on the knapping surface. With another stone in hand, use the Left mouse button to remove all the parts highlighted in orange, to form the chosen tool head.

Tips: To see which stones are hard enough to make tools, check the tooltip in the inventory. Loose stones on the ground can be immediately used for knapping instead of picking them up, if you have another stone in-hand and use Shift + Right mouse. To save time, not all orange voxels need to be removed, only those directly touching the tool head.

Now that you have made a tool head, you'll need to add a handle to it to create your first tool!

Clay forming

Hands-on sculpting. Ever wanted to feel the moist, soft clay as you squeeze it between your fingers?

Clay forming produces many pottery items and also tool molds. As with knapping, hold Shift + Right mouse with clay in hands to create a clay forming surface. A selection of recipes will be offered. Once you have selected a recipe, you have to form it. Use the Left mouse button to remove voxels and the Right mouse button to add voxels. Once the shape is complete, pick it up and fire it in a pit kiln.

Tip: You can select different tool modes (hit F) to add/remove multiple voxels, as well as to copy whole layers of clay with the copy layer mode.

Meal making
Listen to the pot lid rattle

The creation of meals will allow you to subsist for longer on the food you have gathered. Create a bowl and a pot with pottery and fire them in a pit kiln. Once you have a fired pot, place it into a firepit, this will add 4 "cooking pot" slots to the firepit inventory where you can place ingredients. You can cook many different meals by filling 2 - 4 slots of the cooking pot with ingredients. All used slots must hold an equal amount of portions. Portion sizes for each ingredient can be found up in the meal recipes. You can cook up to 6 portions at once, but the more portions, the longer it takes to cook!

If you actually want to eat that meal instead of inhaling the sweet aroma, you will need a bowl. With an empty bowl in hand, Right mouse-click on the pot to fill the bowl. You can then eat from the bowl. If you want to clean out a bowl or cooking pot without eating its contents, just toss it in some water.

You can read the cooking recipes for more specific instructions and lists of ingredients. Alternatively, some simple cooked foods, such as roasted meats or cooked cattail root, require no pot at all, just prepare the item directly over a firepit. And don't forget to check out dough and the pie recipes for lessons in baking, too!

Charcoal burning
Coal. Synonymous to the industrial revolution.

Charcoal is the first source of fuel used to achieve temperatures high enough to smelt metal ores. Charcoal requires a lot of firewood to produce and might require you to chop down a forest or two.

Once you think you have gathered enough firewood, dig a pit. Your charcoal pit can be any dimension up to 11x11x11 blocks, though 2x2x2 should be fine to start with, and it should be made entirely of airtight, noncombustible blocks. Fill your pit with complete stacks of firewood and make sure you leave no empty blocks. Any air pockets will light on fire and your firewood will burn to ash. Cover the filled pit completely with noncombustible blocks, but leave the top of a single stack of firewood exposed to air.

Using dried grass and 4 more firewood, build a firepit on the top of the exposed stack of firewood and light the firepit. Quickly (you have 30 in-game minutes) cover it up with solid blocks to seal the pit. If the pit begins smoking peacefully, you will be rewarded with charcoal in less than an in-game day! If you hear burning sounds, you should open up the pit and quickly extinguish the fire - you must have missed a spot or built a wall out of something that will burn.

Once you have the materials to craft them, the kiln door and iron trapdoor will also work as a solid wall when closed, allowing you to build a more permanent charcoal burning structure with easy access. Just remember to build it out of something that won't burn down!

Farming
It ain't much but it's honest work!

When you've found several seeds, and found a place to settle down, it's time to start farming. There are several factors that play into farming:

Soil Fertility
Soil comes in four levels of fertility; low, medium, high, and 'terra preta'. Try to avoid planting crops in low fertility soil. They may struggle to mature in a timely manner.

Moisture
Crops need moisture to grow. Planting crops within three blocks of water will help them maintain good moisture levels. However, you can grow crops even on ground with no water nearby by using a watering can, or natural rainfall, which will increase soil moisture.

Planting
Once you've selected your location to farm, till the soil using a hoe, and plant your seeds by Right mouse clicking. You should also think about the temperature and nutrient requirements of the seeds.

Soil Nutrients
The tool tip of the tilled farmland will tell you the status of the three soil nutrients (N, P, and K) for that block. Different plants need different nutrients, and will use them up from the soil as they grow. If the required nutrient is low, they will grow much slower. It is good practice to rotate your crops so that each subsequent planting uses a different nutrient than the one before. Farmland will naturally regenerate nutrients over time when left fallow. There are also several types of fertilizer in the world, which can more quickly replenish nutrients.

Temperature
Below 10°C crop growth is slowed, below 0°C crops don't grow at all. Different crops have different tolerances for extreme temperature - both low and high. If a crop is subjected to excessive heat or cold, it may become frost or heat damaged, which will cause it to only give half the yield when you harvest. In extreme temperatures, crops will start to take cold/heat damage, accumulating damage points. The points will go away if the temperature returns to safer levels, however, if the crop accumulates 48 hours of extreme temperature damage, it will die. Dead crops will give a seed (but no other produce) at harvest, unless they died very young, in which case they may yield nothing at all.

Harvesting
Once mature, harvest crops by hand, or with a scythe.

Pests
Certain animals, such as hares, will attempt to eat your crops. It's wise to protect them with a rough-hewn fence or other obstacle.

Food preservation
Summer in a jar!

Preserving food can greatly increase its shelf life. This is particularly valuable in hot climates or during summer, as food spoils quicker in the heat, and for long winters when less food is available. There are several food preservation methods, combining them can have a multiplicative effect.

Cellars
Any fully enclosed space is considered a cellar and will have a low and consistent year-round temperature. The most simple cellar consists of a 1x2x1 hole with a container in it, that's covered up with soil. More elaborate versions can be up to 7x7x7 blocks in size with a door. To verify a cellar is working, look at any container's block info. You will want to reach the lowest possible food perish speed. Build cellar walls from soil, brick or stone materials.

Crocks
You can place meals inside crocks to receive a slight benefit, but sealing crocks with wax or fat further decreases the decay rate 10-fold. To seal a crock, simply place it on the ground and use the sealing item on it. A shelf placed in your cellar makes it easy to organize your crocks.

Storage vessels
A storage vessel is a good place to store grains, grain products such as bread, and raw vegetables.

Pickling
If you have access to salt, you can pickle meat and vegetables in a barrel: look up the recipes in the handbook.

Animal Husbandry
Begin the agricultural revolution!

Sheep, goats, pigs, chickens, and hares can be turned into productive livestock. When you come across them, enclose them in a fenced-in area, chase them to your desired location, or catch them with a basket trap or crate trap if possible. They are also attracted to troughs filled with food. Use a small trough for chickens, hares, and other small animals, and a large trough for pigs, sheep, goats, and other large animals.

Rearing livestock
Feeding animals will make them produce offspring and prevent them from losing weight during winter. Most animals require only a breeding pair to be given enough food and time to reproduce, but poultry (chickens) also require a henbox in which they can lay and incubate their eggs. If there are not enough henboxes the hens will instead lay their eggs on the ground, which will not hatch, but can still be eaten.

Domestication
Animals bred this way will, over several generations, lose their fear and aggressiveness towards the player. Once they have reached the 3rd generation you can also kill them instantly with a cleaver.

Dairy farming
When ewes and nannies have recently given birth they can be milked. The more domesticated they are the more likely they will be to produce milk for you. Milk goes bad quickly so make sure to drink it or use it to produce cheese or it will go to waste!

Beekeeping
In order to obtain wax and honey, you will need to build skeps into which wild bees like to swarm. Be sure to place some flowers around. You can move a populated skep inside a free backpack slot by Right mouse clicking it. Carry it to the desired location and use Ctrl+Scroll wheel to select that backpack slot, to place the skep back down again. Your bees will visit nearby flowers and slowly produce honey, a richly populated skep can also in turn swarm to start a new bee colony in a nearby empty skep. When your skep colony is mature, break it to remove the honeycomb, note that this is quite likely to anger the bees. Angry bees can become diverted if there happens to be anything nearby which could be mistaken for you. Squeeze the honeycomb over an open container or in the fruitpress to extract the honey, leaving wax. Honey can be stored and moved around with any liquid container.

guides.t: Game Mechanic: Panning for ore and more
guides.h:
Panning
There's gold in those hills!

Panning allows the player to obtain small quantities of copper and a few other types of nuggets, as well as other items. It is a useful way to obtain copper nuggets in the early game, if you're not finding enough through exploring.

All the player needs for panning are a wooden pan, water to stand in, and either sand, gravel, or bony soil (muddy gravel will NOT work). Simply stand in the water, Right mouse click the pan on the material to be sifted, and then Right mouse click once to start sifting. Each block of material has eight 'charges' for the pan.

The stone type of sand and gravel makes no difference in results, aside from the stones that you obtain from it. Sand and gravel produce the same results. Bony soil, however, will produce a much different set of results from sand and gravel.

Smelting

Metallurgy 101. Only here on Vintage Story.

To acquire your first metal tools you will need to smelt copper, and later on bronze. You will need charcoal, clay, copper nuggets, and a pair of tongs. Craft a crucible through clay forming and fire it in a pit kiln. You can acquire charcoal through the process of charcoal burning. Before you begin, also prepare and fire one or more tool molds. You might want to start out with a pickaxe and hammer mold. Also don't forget to make a pair of tongs (and hold them in your off hand) to handle the scorching hot metal!

Once prepared, place the crucible in the firepit, then place nuggets into the 4 crucible slots and heat with charcoal. You can place any amount of ore nuggets in the crucible (128 per slot X 4), but the more ore you add, the longer the smelting process will take.

Once smelted, hold your tongs in your off hand, and take the crucible out of the firepit and hold over a mold, press Right mouse to begin pouring. Most molds require 100 units of metal to be complete (each nugget is 5 units). The molten metal will be very hot initially, after the item has cooled to below 200 degrees, you can take out your cast item.

Congratulations! You are now a master metallurgist \o/

Smelting high melting point ores
Some ores, such as quartz, iron ore and meteoric iron have high melting points that cannot be reached using a simple crucible in a firepit. These you will have to smelt in a bloomery + chimney.

Smithing
Got your anvil ready? Time to get real.

Smithing is the way to enter the late copper age and beyond. If you don't have an anvil yet, create an anvil mold through clay forming, fire it and fill it with 900 units of copper or bronze. You will also need a hammer. Smelt some ingots to be forged. Build a forge and fill it with charcoal. Use Right mouse click to place one or two ingots into the forge and ignite with a torch in hand to heat up your ingots to a white-hot temperature. When the ingot is hot enough, take it from the forge, and place it on the anvil. You will be offered recipes, carefully select the one you want to smith. Use the hammer in different tool modes (hit F) to spread the metal into the voxels and remove any excess metal. Additional ingots can be added in the same way if you need more metal.

Congratulations! You are now a master smith \o/

Prospecting
Ready to move on from the copper age?

In order to advance you will have to find some rather rare resources to create bronze. The prospecting pick can help you find where not to search for them. Once you have either poured or smithed a prospecting pick, pack your bags and go for a journey!

Density Search Mode
Break 3 rock blocks in 'close' proximity to "sample" the area for ores. The sampled blocks must be located a minimum of 3 blocks apart and a maximum of 16 blocks apart. You can sample anywhere, as long as you break rock. For example, when you come across a cave, an outcropping of stone, or dig through the dirt to reach solid rock, break one block to start the sampling process. Move at least three blocks and break another block. Do this again to finish collecting your samples.

Once your samples are completed, the chat info log will show you a reading of all prospectable resources at this location. Results are shown as ore densities. A low density resource means you probably want to move on and keep prospecting until you find a medium to high density location, it might also mean you are near the edge of a deposit, so look around to see if you can find a stronger reading. Even a high density reading is no guaranteed certainty to actually find ore. If enabled, you can use the node search mode to locate the individual ore veins underground, if it detects any.

Example Reading
Ultra high Cassiterite (0.3‰)
Very poor Chromite (0.5‰)
Minuscule amounts of Bismuthinite

Interpretation:
Cassiterite is generally found only in small quantities - this area contains about 0.3 per mille, which means roughly 0.3 out of 1000 rock blocks contain this ore if the entire area were to be mined. The reading being ultra high means here you have the best chance in finding this ore. Chromite is found more commonly than tin here - 0.5 per mille, but the reading is very poor because areas can be found with much higher quantities. Minuscule amounts of other ores mean there is still a very low chance you could find this ore in this area.

Additional hints
In the density search mode, the sample results are valid for the entire height of the world, you won't get different readings from sampling above or below. It is generally sufficient to sample only every 30 to 100 blocks away from a previous reading.

Node Search Mode
If the server or game settings allow it, the prospecting pick can instead be set to 'Node Search' mode using the F (tool mode) key with the Propick in hands. In this mode the prospecting pick will probe at a much smaller radius (2 - 8 blocks, configurable through a command), and if it finds something, there is guaranted to be an ore vein within the vicinity. In that case it is only a matter of finding the right direction to mine towards...

Temporal Stability
The world is in a constant state of flux.

The cyan gear between your health and hunger bar is your temporal stability meter. Staying in areas of low stability will drain your temporal stability, which is indicated by your gear turning counter-clockwise. If your temporal stability reaches zero, you will enter the rust world, where tough enemies are more likely to spawn and you will take constant damage. Certain areas, especially deep underground are temporally unstable. If your temporal stability is dropping when on the surface, you might want to find another place to settle down. Sometimes you will encounter temporal storms on the surface, which have the same effect as having low temporal stability. When a temporal storm is approaching, the chat box will let you know, so you have time to prepare.

Ways to increase your temporal stability:
- Enter a temporally stable area, which is indicated by your gear turning clockwise
- Killing drifters will recover small amounts of temporal stability
- Putting a temporal gear in your left hand, a knife in your main hand and holding Right mouse will transfer temporal stability from the gear to you, but consumes the gear and some of your health.

Rifts
Rifts are portals to the rust world that appear at random on the surface, which spawn drifters and cause your temporal stability to drop greatly when up close. They disappear on their own after 1 or 2 ingame days. The amount of appearing rifts depend on the current global rift activity. Torch light currently deters rift apperances, in case you want to make your base more rift-proof.

Armor
So you can take a hit.

Choosing the right armor is the difference between winning or losing. Low tier armor breaks quickly against high tier attacks, whereas high tier armor can become very costly - each have their up- and downsides. Here's a lineup:

Shields
The cheapest form of protection is a shield, such as the a crude shield.

Improvised armor
The earliest type of armor you can make. Only protects your body while leaving your head and legs exposed. It can only take a few hits before it breaks, but nonetheless can save your life in dire times.

Lamellar armor
Somewhat more effort to due to the requirement of pelts, but offers greater protection while still relatively low cost to create. You can create lamellar armor from wood, copper or bronze.

Leather armor
Offers a good balance between flexibility and protection.

Gamboised armor
Created by layering lots of linen. Takes an immense amount of linen to create, but therefore offers great protection without losing too much flexibility.

Brigandine armor
Heavy metal armor. Great protection at the cost of reduced flexibility. You can create brigandine from copper, bronze or iron.

Chain armor
While chain is a lot of effort to smith, it's offering great protection while still being quite lightweight. You can create chain armor from copper, bronze or iron.

Scale armor
Heavy duty armor. Close to impenetrable but also costly in material and flexibility. You can create scale armor from copper, bronze or iron.

Plate armor
Turns you into a walking tank. The highest tier, steel plate armor, makes you practically invulnerable. But be sure to bring lots of food with you and don't expect to escape a battle while wearing it.

Mechanical Power
The mechanical work horse is the path to prosperity.

Mechanical power can currently be used to mechanize milling, to automate working iron blooms or smithing any type of metal plate, and to power the Archimedes screw for transporting items. You will need to craft one windmill rotor, at least 4 sails as well as a few axles and gears. The windmill requires at least 5 blocks of vertical space and usually gets more wind the higher it is, so begin by placing the rotor on a tower or the side of a tall building. The back of the windmill rotor will be attached to axles and gears to bring power to your machine.

Other Power Sources: In addition to a regular windmill, you can build a water wheel on rapidly flowing rivulets (usually found in hills and mountains). Once you reach iron age, you can also build a metal windmill rotor, which can be up to twice the diameter of a regular windmill. Remember to place windmills of any size at least one and one half times their diameter away from other windmills to avoid turbulence, which will reduce the power output!

For mechanized milling: Craft a quern from any igneous rock, then use axles and gears to connect the rotor to either the top or bottom of the quern to be automated. If the quern's output slot is full or occupied, the quern will begin to drop items on each of its 4 sides. Placing a block beside the quern will prevent the quern from dropping items on the blocked side, but reduces the grinding efficiency. You can use this fact to place hoppers and chests below the sides of the quern to catch quern output. Placing one hopper above the quern allows you to grind multiple stacks of material automatically.

For mechanized smithing: Smith or cast a helve hammer head, the helve hammer itself, a base and a wooden toggle. Using the gears and axles connect the output of your windmill rotor to the left or right side of the wooden toggle. Place the helve hammer base adjacent to the toggle. Place an anvil (it must be bronze tier or higher) three blocks away from the base and then attach the helve hammer onto the base. If you add an optional brake it must be placed on the free side of the helve hammer base (opposite the axle bringing in power). Note! A helve hammer will only smith metal plates, refine iron blooms, and hammer blister steel into ingots. Tools and weapons cannot be smithed using the helve hammer.

To sharpen weapons: Construct a grinding wheel and place it on the end of a powered shaft. The grinding wheel is a pass-through machine, so you can have it in the middle of a shaft that goes to something else.

To power the machine you have built: Right mouse click on the windmill rotor to add the sails. Each set of 4 sails will add 20% power output to the windmill. When there is enough wind, the windmill will turn and the machine will begin to move. A windmill with more sails will begin turning at lower wind speeds, as a certain amount of power is needed to get the quern and helve hammers moving.

Larger and more complex builds can be created using the large wooden gear. Combined with standard gears it can either speed up rotation (but with weaker torque) or slow down rotation (but with much stronger torque). It can also bring together torque from several windmills or other power sources. Optionally, you can use a transmission with a clutch next to it, to temporarily interrupt a power train. A brake can stop a power train completely. Spur gears are an additional option for transferring and splitting power.

Steelmaking
Scorching hot ovens abound, telltale signs of industry

The earliest form of steel, Blister Steel, requires the construction of a cementation furnace. This structure is used to slowly enrich iron with carbon (carburization).

Construction
Building a cementation furnace requires around 65 blocks of refractory bricks, which come in 3 different qualities: tier 1, tier 2 and tier 3. Each tier is more robust against heat damage than the last. You will also need 6 refractory brick gratings and a solid or windowed iron door. Build two stone coffin sections and two stone coffin lids from either granite, andesite, basalt or peridotite. Place a 3x2 flooring of grating. In the middle of it, place both stone coffin sections in opposing directions, so as to create a large container. With a Shift + Right mouse click on the stone coffin you will see an outline showing where you have to place the remaining refractory bricks and the iron door. You can add additional refractory bricks on the outside of the structure, if you wish, but keep the air pathways in the interior of the structure clear.

Firing
Once that is ready, fill the stone coffin to the top with 16 iron ingots and charcoal or coke. Then, dig out an empty space two blocks below each stone coffin section - this is where you have to place 2 piles of coal (or charcoal) in order to fire the furnace. You can use a chisel to build a small retaining wall so that the coal doesn't fall to the sides while piling. Once all is ready, ignite the coal piles.

You can verify the furnace is working by looking into it through the door (but we don't recommend you go inside there, it's quite hot!) Fire particles should emanate from the burning coal and smoke should exit from the chimney. You will need to replenish and re-light the coal piles approximately once a day, but leave the stone coffin closed. Firing will take about one week in total, after which you can break the stone coffin to get blister steel.

Refining
Blister steel needs to be worked on an iron anvil to create steel. You can create an iron anvil by smithing the bottom and top halfs on a bronze anvil. Place the parts on the ground on top of each other with some flux in between, then hammer a few times to create the iron anvil.

Coke oven
Coke is to coal what charcoal is to wood. Coke is produced by 'burning' coal in an oxygen-less environment, such as a coke oven.

A coke oven is a multi-block structure, made of fireclay bricks or any type of refractory bricks, and an iron hatch door. The oven is essentially a 3x3x3 cube of refractory bricks, with the center empty, and one of the four cardinal directions from the center also empty. In the center you place the coal layers, and in the adjacent empty space, an iron hatch door. Ignite the coal with a torch and close the door - in 12 hours it will be converted to coke. Coke burns at very high temperatures, though not for as long as raw coal.

Weather
Not only looks pretty, it also affects gameplay.

Weather in Vintage Story is location based, so you will experience more rain in Jungles and less in Deserts. Rain and snow will have the following effects on the game world:
- Make your farmland moist so crops can grow.
- Extinguishes firepits, torches and forges
- Cools down any hot work items on forges and anvils.

Blocks extinguished by rainfall can be relit using a torch.

There are three general types of stone in Vintage Story:

Sedimentary stone types include Claystone, Sandstone, Limestone, Chalk, Shale, Chert, Conglomerate, and Bauxite.
Sedimentary layers will always occur above igneous and metamorphic stone layers (except basalt, which is an exception). So for instance if you are searching for limestone or chalk, and you see the top stone layer of an area is igneous or metamorphic, then look elsewhere - there will not be sedimentary below. However if the top layer is another sedimentary stone, it is possible that different sedimentary layers are below - perhaps find a cave and investigate deeper.

Metamorphic stone types include Phyllite and Slate, as well as marble. Marble however only occurs as deposits within Phyllite or Slate. Metamorphic layers will always occur below sedimentary layers, but above igneous layers.

Igneous stone types include Andesite, Granite, Peridotite, and Basalt. Igneous layers always occur below sedimentary and metamorphic layers (except basalt, which is an exception and can occur above ANY other stone layer). If the top layer of stone in an area is igneous (other than basalt) then you know that there are no sedimentary or metamorphic layers below.

Searching for limestone or chalk? They are not any more or less likely to occur based on climate or any other factor, but are simply random. Just be sure to pay attention to the top stone layer, and if it is sedimentary or basalt, you might want to investigate caves in the area to make sure there is not more sedimentary layers below.

Searching for bauxite? Bauxite, like all stone layers, is not linked to any particular geography or climate. Explore and you should eventually find it! Being sedimentary, it will always be above metamorphic and igneous layers (except basalt).

Cheese Making
Making cheese is a lengthy but rewarding process, that can be broken down into four steps:

Step 1: Fill a barrel with either 25 or 50 litres of milk, and add pickled vegetables of any sort. Seal the barrel, and in time the milk will curdle.

Step 2: Add salt to the curdled mlik and seal the barrel. In time this will create cottage cheese (You can use a bowl to eat the cottage cheese).

Step 3: Use a piece of linen to remove the cottage cheese from the barrel. Place the bundle on the ground, and add a stick. Twist the curd bundle until all the whey is removed. Open the curd bundle, and add 5 salt to the exposed cheese wheel.

Step 4: At this point you can either place the salted raw cheese wheel on a shelf to cure, or craft it in your grid with a piece of wax to turn it into a waxed raw cheese wheel, which will last longer. Place the salted/waxed cheese wheel on a shelf to cure. After many days, you will have cheddar cheese!

Blue Cheese: To make blue cheese, you must store the raw cheese in an enclosed with a very cold, very low light level cave with at least one block open to the outside.

Ferrous metal (iron, meteoric iron, and steel) tool and weapon heads can obtain extra properties if properly quenched and/or tempered. Non-ferrous metals cannot gain bonuses (or penalties) from these processes.

Quenching
Quenching can be done with, or without, a layer of fire clay being added to the item. With clay, the durability will be improved. Without clay, the power level will be improved.
Successful quenching can only be done starting from a certain temperature range, as shown in the tooltip of the item. When the item has reached this range, you may toss it in a block of liquid, or Right mouse while looking at a block of water or barrel of quenchant liquid (as of 1.22 water is the only valid quenchant). You must swiftly bring the temperature down to below 100C.
Quenching does cause stresses in the metal, in the form of a percent chance to shatter if quenched again. You can quench an item an unlimited number of times, but the shatter chance will go up consistently, while the benefits gained will decrease in magnitude each time. The shatter risk only applies to quenching, not tempering.
After quenching, the bonus obtained will be shown in the tooltip, as will the number of times this piece was properly quenched. If the item shatters during quenching, the item and all its metal will be lost.

Tempering
The tempering process is used to reduce the shatter chance that quenching adds to the item. Similar to quenching, the tempering process involves bring the work piece up to a specific temperature range, and then cooling it. It differs from quenching, in that the temperature is lower, and the rate of cooling must be much slower than quenching. Allowing the item to simply cool in the air while held or placed is sufficient
Successful tempering will reduce the shatter chance slightly. If your tempering improved the durability of the blade, that durability will remain unchanged. However if your quenching improved the power, the power will also go down slightly. The shatter chance will go down more though, as a percentage of the total. One cannot temper an item more times than it has been quenched.

Where to Find
Fruit trees can be found throughout the world, in virtually all climates. Different climates will have different types of trees. Not all fruit trees can survive in all climates.

Growth Habits
Fruit trees start small, but over a long time period will get very large, bit by bit; they do not instantly grow to maturity like regular trees.
They only bear fruit once a year, and this time will vary by the type. They will go through stages of flowering, fruit bearing, and fruit ripening. Trees of temperate climates will go through a dormancy period where they have no leaves.

Propagation
You can propagate fruit trees by removing a branch to get a cutting, and then planting the cutting on dirt, or placing the cutting onto the cut branch stub of another fruit tree. Only a portion of grafts will succeed, and an even smaller number of planted cuttings.

guides.t: Crafting Mechanic: Brewing and Distilling Alcohol
guides.h:
Fermenting
The initial step of making alcohol is to ferment your raw material in a barrel. You can ferment fruit juices (which will require a fruit press), honey, and flour (which will require a quern) with water. The result will be a cider, wine, ale, or mead, depending on the raw material used.

Distilling
The next step of alcohol making is distilling. For this you will need a boiler and a condenser. The boiler can only be fueled with firewood. Place a bucket under the condenser spout, fill the condenser with water, and build a firepit under the boiler. Fill the boiler with up to 30L of fermented alcohol, and light the fire under the boiler. After a time, the fermented alcohol will be converted to a distilled spirit, such as brandy, whiskey, or vodka.

Aqua Vitae
Repeat the distilling process once more, but with spirits rather than fermented alcohol. The product of this will be nearly pure alcohol, called Aqua Vitae, which can be used as an ingredient for useful items.

Mordants
In order to hold its color, cloth needs to be treated in a chemical solution called a mordant before it is dyed. Mordants can be made from different materials. Once you've found a good material for it (through prospecting or trading), you'll need to crush it with a pulverizer and add it to a barrel of water. Then you're ready to add your cloth to the barrel and seal it for a few hours.

Dyeing
Dyes can be made out of many different plants and minerals. Some of these will be easier to find than others. Once you've found the pigment you're looking for, you can add it to a barrel of water to make a dye. Some dyes require more pigment than others. Once your barrel of dye is ready, just add mordanted cloth to it and seal it for a while and you'll have vivid, colorful cloth to make clothes (Note: many of the finer clothes require a tailor to make them).

Direct dyes
Some materials, such as woad or tannin, naturally bond to fibers and therefore do not require a mordant. If your technology hasn't progressed enough to find mordants or build a pulverizer, try using one of these direct dyes.

Ground Storage
Many items and most tools can be stored on the ground; this can be especially helpful in the early game when storage containers can be scarce. If an item is able to be stored this way, it will be indicated on the handbook page.

Storing On Flat Ground
Items such as cooking pots, bowls, crucibles, and even shoes and boots, can be stored on a flat surface; up to four per block space, one in each quadrant. To place an item this way, have the item selected in the hotbar, hold the Shift key and Right mouse click to place the item. Pick up again with an empty hand and Right mouse click.

Leaning Against A Wall
Tools, however, must be leaned against a wall to be stored on the ground, and only two will fit per block. For leaning, you must hold both Shift and Ctrl keys, and then Right mouse click on a flat surface that is next to a vertical block face to place the tool. Right mouse click with an empty hand to pick up again.

Leather making is a multi-step process, that will require at least one barrel, but having several will make the process much faster. You will need some additional materials, as noted below, that are good to prepare ahead of time.

Step 1 - After you have obtained some raw hides, seal them in a barrel of limewater or diluted borax for 24 hours.
Step 2 - Remove the now soaked hide and craft them in the grid with a knife, to get a scraped hide.
Step 3 - Seal the scraped hides in a barrel of weak tannin for 3 days.
Step 4 - Remove the prepared hides from the weak tannin, and place them in a barrel of strong tannin for 4.5 days. After that time, the hides will turn to leather, with larger hides yielding more pieces.

Greenhouses

Once you have obtained glass, you can make a greenhouse to extend your growing season. Any farmland, fruit tree or berry bush inside the greenhouse will receive a +5 degree temperature boost.

The maximum interior volume on a single greenhouse is 14x14x14 blocks. The roof of the greenhouse must be at least 50% glass (full block or slab, can also be chiseled glass as long as one side is solid). The walls can be of any material, and can be shared between greenhouses. If you use glass slabs for roof or walls, the base or main 'flush' side (matching other blocks) must be oriented inward.

Beehive Kiln

A beehive kiln allows you to fire large amounts of clay items at once. Similar to the Cementation Furnace, the Beehive Kiln requires a door: the kiln door. Place the door, and then Ctrl + Right mouse click on it, and a 'blueprint' of ghost blocks will appear. The kiln has three required types of blocks: refractory bricks, refractory brick gratings, and iron hatch doors. Regular fireclay brick versions of the blocks, gratings, and kiln door can also be used, but will degrade faster.

The interior volume of the kiln is 3x3x3 blocks. The floor of this space must be composed of nine refractory gratings. You also have the option to place refractory gratings in the middle layers of the space, which acts as shelving for a second level of clay products. Three iron hatch doors are required, and must be placed one in each of the other walls that don't have the kiln door.

Directly below each of the nine floor gratings, must be placed a pile of fuel - the piles do not need to be completely full, but you need at least some fuel in all 9 spots. You can use any stackable fuel from wood to coal. The walls and floor of this fuel chamber can be any material. Once you have filled the kiln with clay products, ignite the fuel piles and close the door. After several cycles, there will be a chance for the refractory bricks to become damaged and require replacement, similar to the cementation furnace. This wear will accumulate whenever fuel is burning in all nine spots, so it is best to only use as much fuel as necessary to finish your batch. After the cycle is finished, the clay products will be hot and require tongs to handle.

Producing Colored Ceramics
The iron hatch doors in the kiln walls are used to control the color of ceramics produced by the kiln. The more of the iron hatch doors you have open, the more oxygen will reach the fuel, and the darker the final color of the ceramics will be. In this way, you can get as many as four different ceramic colors from a single type of clay.

Sailboat Construction

Constructing a sailboat requires a great deal of materials, and many steps. But it all starts with simple rollers. Craft five rollers and select them in your hotbar: an in-world schematic will appear. You can change the direction the schematic faces using the F key. Place the rollers on a flat area (making sure the blue highlighted schematic strip is in water).

Afterward, if you have block interaction help turned on (toggle with blockinteractionhelp), looking at the in-process boat will show you the next required ingredients. You will need logs and boards of the same species of tree. Beyond that you will need more firewood, two plumb-and-squares, and rope. Once you have completed and launched the boat, you can also add ratlines to allow you to climb to the top of the mast. See the sailboat handbook entry for more information on how to equip your new sailboat.
You can deconstruct the sailboat to get a portion of the materials back, by Right mouse it with a saw. You will have to hold the mouse button down for some time, before this will be completed.

Tamed Mountable Animals

Certain animals, such as Elk, can be tamed and used as mounts. Mounted animals have several locations to add tack and equipment:
Saddle- In order to ride your mount, you will need a saddle. It is placed on a location directly above the back.
Saddle blanket- Saddle blankets are an optional accessory. They are placed on a location on the upper part of the back, below the saddle location.
Bridle- There are two bridle options: curb and snaffle. The snaffle bit will allow you to control the mount in the same way the character is controlled.
The curb bit will use a control scheme where you press the forward key once, and the mount will continue moving without holding the key.
Saddlebags- Saddlebags may be placed just above the rear legs, over the haunches, to provide extra inventory space.
Hay bed- A hay bed may be placed on top of the animal's rump, directly behind the saddle.
Lantern- A lantern may be hung from the mount's neck.
Utility locations - There are two locations (left and right) over the front shoulders, where the player can store a cooking pot.
Temporal Gear Storage - on the right side, directly behind the saddlebags, are three locations for storing temporal gears.
Bone Flute - You can use a bone flute to call a mount to you, so long as it is in a loaded chunk. (This can be used to get the mount out of holes or other stuck spots)

How To Tame
A tamed Elk can be obtained by trapping a wild baby elk (using a crate trap) and taming it. Alternatively, you may purchase one from a treasure hunter trader (after completing the first main story event).

If you capture a baby elk, you then must keep it and feed it well for a year, at which point it will grow into a 'semi-tamed' animal. At this point you must repeat a cycle of placing a saddle on it, mounting it, and riding it till bucked off. After doing this a number of times, the animal will become tamed.

Equipment you will need
Getting started with fishing is very simple. You need only a fishing pole, bait, and a large body of water. You can make a worm grunter to get worms, or cook up some stink bait - both these baits will catch a wide array of smaller fish. You can also use raw meats, and smaller fish. You can even use no bait at all, but it will take a very long time to catch fish that way. Refer to the handbook entry for the fishing poles and the worm grunting stick to see how to use them.
With bait and a pole, you're ready to go find the fish!

Finding The Fish
Finding where the fish are is the most time-consuming step. Fish are of course divided into fresh and saltwater species, but both types use the same baits and are fished for in the same manner. There do not need to be visible fish present - if there are, they will respond to your bait if it lands close. But otherwise you will still get bites and fish, even if no visible fish are present. The body of water in which you fish should be fairly large. Small puddles are unlikely to have fish.
Each species of fish is present in certain climatic ranges, and even within that range they do not cover 100% of the map. In more moderate climates there should be enough fish types around that the odds of having no fish in a spot are very low, but at the extreme hot and cold ends (especially cold) there are fewer viable species, and the chance of having a dead zone of no fish is higher.

Using The Right Bait
Certain fish will only bite on certain types of bait. In general, worms will catch smaller fish, stink bait will catch small and medium fish, and the largest fish will only be caught with meat, or dead fish as bait (there are exceptions though). There are much fewer large fish species, so if you use bait that only large fish will bite on, you are much more likely to encounter 'dead zones' where no large species are. But if you switch to another bait, you might still catch smaller fish.
Juvenile fish - even of the large species - will generally bite on baits that smaller fish bite on. So a possible tactic is to use smaller baits, and note the areas where you catch juvenile versions of large species. Then you can come back to those spots with larger bait to try to catch the adults. You can also catch small fish in that spot, and then use them as bait for the larger fish.

Why Am I Not Catching Fish?
It is important to realize that a location can become 'fished out' if you catch a large number of fish in a short period of time. Fish populations do recover over time, including if you totally 'fish out' an area. Note that there are currently no mechanics that make fish respond to things like temperature, weather, or seasons, and the type of fish found in a given spot will not change over time.
If the area is not fished out, then you may not be catching fish because the species that are present, do not like the bait you are using. Otherwise, there may be actually no fish present in this area, in which case you'd need to move to another spot.
Note that there is intentionally no message to tell you when an area is fished out, or just has no fish. It is up to you to decide if you're not catching fish due to using the wrong bait, being in the wrong spot, or the area being fished out.

The bigger the collector, the less often you have to empty it: that is all it brings to a large plantation.

Capacity
Ceramic: 4
Copper: 8
Bronze: 12
Iron: 16
Steel: 24

The collector material only affects its storage capacity. It does not increase the tree's resin production rate. The rate still depends on temperature, season, tree fatigue and species (pine ×1, acacia ×0.5): a steel collector on an acacia still produces at ×0.5, it simply stores more resin before it is full. Every unit of resin tires the tree the same way, whatever the collector.

Three bronzes
Tin bronze, bismuth bronze and black bronze each make their own collector: same capacity (12), same behaviour, only the look changes. Use whichever bronze you have.

Crafting (the hammer wears, it is not used up)
- Tapping spout: hammer, metal plate and nails and strips of the same metal, one above the other; makes 2 spouts (copper, bronzes, iron, steel).
- Resin collection vessel: nails and strips, hammer and nails and strips above a plate of the same metal (bronzes, iron, steel).
- Copper collector: fired resin pot, copper tapping spout, copper nails and strips and a hammer.
- Bronze collector: vessel and spout of the same bronze, a plank and a hammer.
- Iron and steel collectors: vessel and spout of the same metal, planks treated with resin varnish and a hammer.

Look
Copper: ceramic pot banded with copper. Bronze: pail with a rolled rim and riveted bands. Iron: covered pail, banded and reinforced with corner irons, on a nailed treated board. Steel: covered pail with a funnel, riveted base and handle, on a bolted treated board.

Swapping collectors
Shift + right click removes the collector (its resin is given back), then right click with the new one. The tapping wound, species and tree fatigue are kept.

Default capacities, adjustable by the server.

Copper pipes carry only liquids: turpentine and resin varnish. Resin and rosin stay solid items: use hoppers, chutes and the resin storage bin.

Getting started
1. Place a liquid tank: its input is on the left and its output on the right, seen from the front. The pipe wrench changes the role of a side: Disabled, Input, Output.
2. Set the input of the destination tank and the output of the source (the still's output is its right side, seen from the front; a barrel connects on any side).
3. Lay copper pipes from the source: they connect by themselves.
4. Place the mechanical pump: it draws on the left and pushes on the right (arrow on the base); the wrench swaps it.
5. Connect the pump to vanilla mechanical power through its shaft, at the front or back: water wheel, windmill, axles, gears.
6. Connect the pump output to the destination input with pipes.
7. Start the machinery: liquid flows as soon as the shaft turns. Look at the pump: its state explains what is blocking.

Diagram
Still → Pipe → Pump → Pipe → Tank
Tank → Pump → Pipe → Barrel

Rules
- Flow: 0.25 L/s at water wheel speed, proportional to speed, 1 L/s at most.
- Pipes store nothing: breaking a pipe loses no liquid, the transfer simply stops.
- A network carries one liquid at a time: turpentine and varnish never mix.
- Priority: the source, then the destination, closest to the pump.
- Range: 32 pipe blocks between source and destination, 16 blocks of lift at most, 256 pipes per network.
- The still never receives liquid through pipes, nor does a sealed barrel.

Default values, adjustable by the server.

guides.t: Gemmage: from resin to treated wood
guides.h:
1. Resin. Tap a mature pine with a tapping knife and install a resin pot: resin flows over the days, depending on temperature, season and tree fatigue. Acacia trees can also be tapped, but their resin yield is roughly half that of pine trees. Copper, bronze, iron and steel collectors hold more resin without making the tree produce faster: see Advanced Collectors.

2. Still. The resin still distills 4 resin into 3 rosin and 0.5 L of turpentine.

3. Varnish. In a barrel, 2 rosin and 0.5 L of turpentine make rosin paste; with 0.5 L of linseed oil, sealed for 8 hours, it becomes 1 L of resin varnish.

4. Treated wood. The varnish brush applies 0.05 L of varnish per planks, plank slab or plank stairs block: species and orientation are kept, the wood takes longer to break and is used for the tank, the pump and iron and steel collectors.

5. Storage. The resin storage bin holds 128 resin or 128 rosin, one product at a time (hoppers and chutes accepted); the liquid tank holds 20 L of turpentine or varnish and never mixes them.

6. Automation. Copper pipes and a mechanical liquid pump driven by a water wheel or windmill carry turpentine and varnish: still → pipe → pump → pipe → tank, 0.25 L/s. The pipe wrench sets connections and swaps the pump; full details in Liquid automation.

Other rosin uses. Pitch glue in a cooking pot (2 rosin and 1 charcoal powder) and resin firestarters.

Default amounts, adjustable in the server configuration.

Resin Storage Bin: solid storage, up to 128 resin or 128 rosin. It accepts one product at a time and unlocks once empty. Shift + right click stores one item (Shift + Ctrl: the whole held stack), right click takes out one item (Ctrl: a stack). Hoppers store from above and take out from below. When broken, its contents drop.

Liquid Tank: 20 L liquid storage for turpentine or resin varnish. It never mixes liquids: empty it completely to switch. Right click with a bucket, jug or bowl to pour or draw (Ctrl: one portion only). When broken, it keeps its liquid in the item. Its graduated window shows the level.

Recipes: bin = 6 planks and 2 copper nails and strips. Tank = 4 treated planks, a copper plate, 2 copper nails and strips, a barrel and a glass block.

The tank's copper fittings (input on the left, output on the right) connect to copper pipes: see "Liquid automation".

Default capacities, adjustable by the server.

The Basics
Cannabis seeds can be planted on tilled farmland. Plants grow through 8 stages. Harvest at stage 8 for buds and seeds. Stage 7 yields seeds, fan leaves, and a small chance of buds. Seeds can also be found growing wild in the right climates.
Add quality to your crop through advanced techniques. Enjoy your crop for buffs and effects.

Strains
Hindu Kush - Found in temperate forests and grasslands. Tolerates cold well. -8°C to 36°C.
Effects: Healing, hunger reduction, foraging.

Red Congo - Found in hot, wet jungle and rainforest climates. Needs warmth and moisture. 7°C to 46°C.
Effects: Ranged accuracy, ranged damage.

Mazar-i-Sharif - Found in cold mountain regions and dry upland terrain. Thrives where other strains fail. -18°C to 30°C.
Effects: Temporal stability, movement speed.

Acapulco Gold - Found in hot, arid desert and savanna regions with little rainfall. 6°C to 50°C.
Effects: Mining speed, ore drops.

Advanced Techniques
Three steps improve quality from Poor to Dank:
Fertilizing - Craft Cannabis Fertilizer and apply to a stage 1 or 2 plant.
Rack Drying - Hang wet buds on a Cannabis Drying Rack. Up to 9 buds of the same strain. Collect after 48 in-game hours.
Jar Curing - Place dry buds in a Cannabis Jar and sneak+right-click to seal. Ready after 72 in-game hours. Cured buds spoil much more slowly.

Quality
Poor - no processing (0.5x)
Fine - one step (0.75x)
Good - two steps (1.0x)
Dank - all three steps (1.35x)
These quality modifiers increase your strain's effects. Aim for the highest to get the most out of your crop.

Grow Tonic
Grow Tonic adapts any strain to any climate, overriding temperature requirements entirely. Also speeds up growth by about 25%. Apply to a freshly planted crop. Reapply after each harvest. Has 20 uses.

Joints, Pipes, and Bongs
Joints - Rolled from bud. Hold right-click to smoke.
Pipes - Pack from your offhand, light on a heat source, then wear it and smoke with the Smoke hotkey. ('R' by default)
Bongs - Assembled from a bowl, body, and stem. Make your parts from any clay, fire them into whatever color you want with a beehive kiln! Mix and match colors! Pack from your offhand, light on a heat source, hold right-click to smoke.

Uses
Buds can used to gain buffs when smoked. Leaves and buds can be extra firepit fuel.

Mature cannabis plants also drop hemp stalks, which can be processed into fibers, twine, linen, and cloth. Stalks can also give hurd for building materials. See Grassroots Hemp Production for details.

Hemp Processing Chain
Hemp stalks are a byproduct of harvesting mature cannabis crops at stage 7 or higher. Stalks break down into fibers in the crafting grid. To obtain hemp hurd, place stalks on ground and use shift+knife to strip stalk. For larger amounts, ret the stalks instead: seal them with water in a barrel and leave them for 24 hours.

Hemp Fibers
Fibers can be made into twine, linen, and cloth.
Plain hemp cloth is dyed in a barrel with a dye and a mordant. Some colors need the mordant step first.
Fibers or twine soaked in water in a barrel make pulp, and can be pressed through a sieve into paper.
With Immersive Fibercraft installed, stalks, fibers, and twine can go through the spinning wheel and loom instead of the crafting grid.

Hemp Oil
Cannabis seeds from any strain can be pressed for hemp oil in a fruit press. Put the seeds in, screw the press down, and the oil collects in the container below. The press holds 10 litres, which takes about 20 seeds to fill.
What is left behind is hemp seed mash. You only get the full amount of mash once all the oil has been pressed out of it.
Hemp oil stands in for rendered fat in several recipes.

Flour and Bread
Hemp seed mash can be ground into hemp flour in a quern. Mix the flour with a litre of water to make hemp dough, then bake the dough in an oven to make hemp bread. Like any bread, it passes through part-baked and perfect stages, and will char if left in too long.

Animal Feed
Seal 0.5 litres of hemp oil with a hemp seed mash in a barrel. After 12 hours you get four hemp seed cake. It can be placed in either size of trough.

Hempcrete
Hemp can be made into a building material that needs no kiln, just time. Seal a litre of limewater with four hemp hurd in a barrel and leave it for 48 hours to get hempcrete mix.
A single mix casts into two hempcrete bricks.

Changing the look
Blocks come in running, soldier and header bonds. Rearrange blocks in the crafting grid to switch between them: two side by side for running, two stacked for soldier, four in a square for header. Three in a row makes uneven bricks, and three stacked turns them back.
Adding a mix to a block doubles its courses. To nudge the brick joints without changing the bond, use a wrench on a placed block.

See Grassroots Cannabis Cultivation for growing, strains, quality and smoking.

Ithania Canned Goods
An overview of everything included in the canning mod.

Ithania Canned Goods adds a full food preservation system built around two tracks: Metal Cans and Glass Jars. Both share the same Canning Bench for filling but use different equipment for sealing and processing, and offer different levels of preservation depending on the materials used.

Items
────────────────────────
Empty Can Empty Can
Steel Can Steel Can
Steel Lid Steel Can Lid
Canning Lid Can Lid
Empty Glass Jar (Plain) Empty Glass Jar
Wooden Jar Lid Wooden Jar Lid
Metal Jar Lid Metal Jar Lid

Blocks
────────────────────────
Canning Bench - Oak Canning Bench
Canning Press - Oak Canning Press
Pressure Cooker Pressure Cooker
Steel Canning Pot Canning Pot

Tools
────────────────────────
Can Opener Can Opener
Steel Canning Tongs Canning Tongs

Metal Cans
────────────────────────
Metal Cans offer the highest preservation available in this mod at ~25x the normal spoil rate once fully processed. They go through several stages — forging, tinning, filling, pressing, and pressure cooking — before becoming a Preserved Can. See the Can States & Preservation Process guide for full details.

Glass Jars
────────────────────────
Glass Jars come in 12 color variants. They use the same Canning Bench for filling and are processed in the Canning Pot rather than the Pressure Cooker. Preservation level depends on the lid used — Wooden Lid (~10x), Wooden Lid with Beeswax (~12x), or Metal Lid (~15x). See the Glass Jars & Preservation guide for full details.

Hot System
────────────────────────
Both cans and Glass Jars retain heat after coming out of their respective cookers. Canning Tongs are needed to handle them safely while hot. Glass Jars in particular can shatter if dropped or exposed to water while still hot. See the Hot System and Canning Tongs guides for full details.

Processing Stations
────────────────────────
Canning Bench: Used by both to fill Empty Cans and Glass Jars with raw ingredients matching valid Cooking Recipes.

Canning Press: Seals Filled Cans with a Canning Lid before pressure cooking.
